items.question: How do you think about the Gemini project's mission across research and Google's products?
items.object: The Gemini project's research and product mission
items.answer:
The goal of Gemini itself is to create an awesome core model to power the technology that LLMs today are powering all around the world, and we obviously expect this to increase. There's two major centers, one in California and one in London, given the organizations that we come from. That in itself is very interesting. We have the project run 24/7, which is helpful when you train these large models. Then you have to do a few things, right? One of the things we do, of course, is trying to build state-of-the-art technology, showing from a research perspective where the field is coming from and where it's going, and trying to showcase from our own intuitions and ambition what might come next. A prime example of this was the long context that we released earlier in the year: millions of tokens now are able to be processed by our models.

But then of course we also take into consideration all the different needs from the different products that we work with. Google has a lot of product areas, so initially, especially to form the project, we try to focus on critical projects. You see that very much by how Gemini is first surfaced to users or to enterprises. Obviously, Cloud and Enterprise are very important; developers as well. It's super cool to put these models in the hands of creative minds that are going to do things you didn't even anticipate these models could do. Then, very importantly, formerly known as Bard, now Gemini app, which is the chatbot surface of our models. And maybe the last very important piece indeed is Search, which is trying to integrate this technology into their product and has a lot of users.

It's extremely exciting to think, well, the decisions you make at modeling eventually—and eventually means just maybe a couple months after or so—will make it into the users that maybe are signing up for a beta, et cetera. It's super exciting, and it's obviously connected. It's the core of the company, really, especially for the products that require very intelligent AI systems like the ones we're creating today.

items.question: How do you see the relationship between LLM-first chatbots and traditional Search evolving?
items.object: The relationship between LLM-first chatbots and traditional Search
items.answer:
We're sort of experimenting, right? You can think of an LLM-first experience, like the chatbot. Search has a role to play in there because it can be seen as a tool that enhances the answers of your chat experience. It provides citations, a bit more reliance—we know that of course language models can and do hallucinate.

There's that LLM-first point of view, which we are building up; it's kind of more of a new product. And then Search itself, which is obviously embracing and enhancing some of the different query types that could be useful, to do a bit more like summaries, like AI summaries. There's a lot more coming. I think Google actually showcased this year quite a lot of a good breadth of vision of what Search is trying to do with language models. Some of it is not ready, but it's being tested, and obviously feedback is very important.

For now it's hard to think of a convergence, or that one sort of dominates the other. Both right now seem useful in different ways. As a user, you use both, certainly. But I think what is very clear is that even if Search is the initial point where you have a query and you want to research something, it just feels like that experience will tremendously be enhanced by these models. The Search product itself is trying to figure out how to integrate the LLM answers or their capabilities, reasoning capabilities, et cetera. I kind of call it Search integrating LLM, and of course that vice versa is very obvious as well.

items.question: How do you approach the choice between chat and Search from your position on the Gemini model team?
items.object: The Gemini model team's role in Google's product strategy
items.answer: As a core model project, like the Gemini project, we have an open mind. We don't really need to decide one or the other. One of the things of operating at the scale that Google operates is that, yes, we are the research team that builds the models, but then of course the product areas are the ones that are going to drive the strategy, influenced by what the models can do and with input from many of us that have been dreaming about this world.

items.question: What has surprised you about Gemini’s long-context capabilities and the uses people are finding for them?
items.object: Gemini’s long-context capabilities and their emerging uses
items.answer:
I guess maybe the ones that surprised me the most—because initially I even thought this was just a number that you could report—is the fact that infinite context length is coming eventually. I thought, look, this is interesting. We come from a world where we had recurrent neural networks and LSTMs that actually had infinite memory, although they were not very capable. The models in practice never remembered more than a few hundred words or so.

So that was kind of first, that we could make the context length so long. Then seeing the use cases just emerge, even internally, when we were first trying the model. That seems very trivial now in hindsight, but putting a whole one-hour video in and just asking anything feels superhuman. You literally put the video in, and after 10 or 30 seconds—it does take some time to process the context—you can ask anything. Thinking of computer vision as a field, or video question answering, some of these datasets that we come from, they all seem very dwarfed compared to the capability that was in our hands.

Then we put it in the hands of developers and saw amazing demos and things that people could do. Even as mind-blowing as pointing the camera to the screen directly, not even the code, just the letters that appear on the screen, and you can debug like that. You can imagine how future interfaces will be effortless. You just need to point the camera, ask a question, and you get answers.

It's an interesting research problem, of course, but maybe it's not going to be that useful yet. Thinking, "Wow, that's amazing," it's not very mainstream either. We're still trying to discover what this enables. We showed Project Astra, where memory is very important: you get the phone and you just interact with it as if it is an agent. But it's still not very clear what this might be in a few years, although you could imagine the whole web is in the context, or all your personal data, because it's resident in your device, because it's the working memory of the model rather than the weights, in lots of applications. But still, fairly early days. So it surprised me, yet in a way it hasn't fully taken off.

items.question: How do you see very long context windows becoming widely used over the next few years?
items.object: The deployment and adoption of very long context windows
items.answer:
If there's a compelling use case, the technology is not far away from being able to be deployed at that scale. Hardware is also being updated based on what the research developments are. Certainly, in one or two years, the context that is a commodity will definitely be enhanced by a factor—I mean, I don't know, 10x or so—everywhere.

Extremely long context, I think, is going to be a motivational drive, definitely from a research perspective. Deploying it at that scale, some techniques have been explored already, like hierarchical memories, and even RAG is pretty common. We're going to combine this, and probably thanks to the use cases, I expect in the order of one or two years you might see, "Wow, we went another order of magnitude," both from state of the art and what's considered commodity. I'm pretty certain about this. That's again about finding use cases that will be compelling to serve the model that requires more memory. There are certain limitations, of course, but these will be figured out from a technological standpoint, if there's the motivation for sure.

items.question: How do you see the value of hierarchical memories as AI context windows get longer?
items.object: Hierarchical memories for extending AI context
items.answer: I think definitely the efficiency argument to hierarchical memories, to make context even longer, makes a lot of sense, even from just efficiency of learning and retrieving the memory in a sort of coarse-to-fine manner, like an intelligent being like ourselves might do.
quotes: I think definitely the efficiency argument to hierarchical memories, to make context even longer, makes a lot of sense, even from just efficiency of learning and retrieving the memory in a sort of coarse-to-fine manner, like an intelligent being like ourselves might do.

items.question: How do you see the role of hybrid retrieval-based and neural-based methods as models gain longer context windows?
items.object: Hybrid retrieval-based and neural-based methods for processing long context
items.answer: We do have a lot of experience, of course, of retrieval-based methods, definitely at Google, and then combining them with neural-based methods. I think it's a matter of time and finessing the details and the use cases of how much. The problem with retrieval-based methods is they tend to simplify things, to say, "Hey, this whole book is just a single vector," whereas if you upload a whole book into Gemini and ask questions, it can really reason about every single word. So probably finding the middle ground for different use cases is needed, but to me it seems like a feature, not a bug, that we do have a bit of a hybrid mode perhaps going into the future.

items.question: What do you credit for the rapid progress you've seen in artificial intelligence?
items.object: The drivers of progress in artificial intelligence
items.answer: To me, one of the biggest changes I've seen is there's more brains, more different backgrounds coming into the field. I usually tend to assign credit for what has happened to the scale of data and compute, algorithmic advances—you can simplify, but there have certainly been some important ones in the last 10 or 20 years—and accessibility: the software, the open-sourcing efforts. Those have been quite critical to create these exponentials, or linear trends in log scale, that we're seeing now.

items.question: How do you distinguish the deep learning era of 2010–2020 from the era of general models?
items.object: The transition from general learning algorithms to general models
items.answer:
I tend to call maybe 2010 to 2020 the deep learning era. What that era did is it took a set of algorithms that were general: stochastic gradient descent, deep learning neural networks, reinforcement learning. You could think of these as ingredients. They're common; you expand them over the years, but they're certainly the same. Then you apply them to a domain and get extremely good at that domain. We have mastering the game of Go, beating the ImageNet challenge, becoming state of the art in speech recognition and image generation. So that decade is kind of the models themselves are not general, but the algorithms are general. You could take the same algorithm and change the dataset and tweak a couple things, and voila, you get protein folding really enhanced from the traditional methods.

Then the greatest insight came from realizing—and I think that's a lucky factor for us, because it makes communication with these entities much easier—that modeling language turns out to be such a powerful abstraction for generality. The GPT-2 paper, especially post, in the abstract says, "Look, you can solve every task, not one task, by modeling language and perfecting that." The whole field, building up from a lot of years of research, created what is not just reusable algorithms, but actually the model now becomes general.

items.question: How do you assess current models' progress toward AGI?
items.object: Progress toward AGI and the reliability of model reasoning
items.answer:
I think AGI is getting closer. We have powerful models: first in 2010 to 2020, now we have general models. Multimodality has more recently been another amazing breakthrough: these techniques expand not just to language but also to vision, sound, videos, et cetera. That means we have very powerful general models that, from an AGI definition standpoint, start to take many boxes. Reasoning capabilities of the models are there, but I don't think we've perfected making the reasoning very crisp and accurate, so these models would not hallucinate. The model might solve an Olympiad mathematical problem yet fail to discern a very basic puzzle. I think what you do with the model, this reasoning step, has a lot of ideas, experience, and algorithmic advances—we've also done a lot in the last few years over Search and so on—but we haven't quite perfected this.

Then of course the question is to push the frontier and move forward in certain domains at least. We've come a long way. Luckily these models are finding usefulness, so the resources that go into training the models right now have a good feedback loop.

items.question: How do you think language models can turn their existing reasoning capabilities into crisp, accurate reasoning?
items.object: Making language-model reasoning crisp and accurate
items.answer:
We still have this probability distribution that will assign nonzero probability to certain things that would not be deemed correct, although in language there are so many ways to say the same thing correctly. That's why these models shine. At the end of the day they are very efficient ways to integrate over all possible sequences.

It's possible that now, when it's a hard problem, a tricky question that requires deep knowledge, you might be at 95% accuracy. But of course these will create errors, even if it's small. This is deployed to the whole world, so certainly you'll get to see the mistakes. One thought would be you just keep making the models larger, keep improving the algorithm, and you're going to hit a point where the probability of a mistake vanishes. It's possible; we will obviously explore that.

To accelerate that progress, you want to start really exploring the reasoning the model has. By making it more redundant, more logical, by iterating more on these kinds of ideas, you could imagine generating a very small program that runs slowly with the language model at the center and then getting that 99. many nines percent. You're going to do both as an ambitious lab and so on. But that crisply means that this probability of error diminishes. We can always put more compute power. We humans make mistakes, we get tired, et cetera, but these models are powerful; we can put more hard work into inference. The hope is that in that sense they become at least as good as humans.

items.question: How do you view the bitter lesson's claim that scaling learning and search is enough?
items.object: The bitter lesson
items.answer: What we're all aiming to discover is to make the bitter lesson ring true. The bitter lesson states that you scale learning and you scale search, and that's all you have to do as a computer scientist. It's controversial. I certainly like simplicity; I'm a deep learner at heart, so I don't disagree with that. The learning scalability part has been tested and proven quite heavily recently.

items.question: What do you see as the central difficulty with using reward functions to improve language models?
items.object: Imperfect reward functions in language models
items.answer:
Search, at least when you do not have access to a perfect reward, is the current problem we have in language. That's one of the key research areas: how do you assign reward finely to statements that not even you and I might agree to be true? Is the sky blue? At night it's not. Assigning truth, or one or zero, which is required in games, is not so applicable here.

If you look at today, most compute is spent in pre-training, and in fact you will see over and over that you overfit. You have to stop the reinforcement learning process to avoid overfitting to these imperfect reward functions. Otherwise you start doing a bit of adversarial search against a reward function that might be imperfect, because you have a dataset of human preferences and all of a sudden the model might discover, "Hey, you can issue lots of emoticons and this reward function thinks that's great." Clearly we have a problem of reward functions not being as accurate as in the game of Go or chess.

items.question: How do you think compute should be divided among pre-training, reinforcement learning, and inference as language models develop?
items.object: The allocation of compute across pre-training, reinforcement learning, and inference
items.answer:
Historically, if you look at AlphaGo, which followed quite closely the recipe of pre-training your model on all human data, then using RL to make it better, and then doing some search at inference time, the compute there was very skewed for the middle step, the reinforcement learning step. I don't know the exact numbers, but certainly the majority of compute was spent on training the self-play, as we called it at the time, self-improvement loop.

Then there's the third component: now you have your model trained, how much do you let it ponder? In AlphaGo, using the same example, the rules say—don't quote me—but roughly a game must last four hours of compute time from a human perspective, so we had quite limited inference time because we obviously couldn't go over time. There was parallelism involved, but the compute there was certainly not as big as the one used to train.

That balance feels correct to me: some on pre-training, and here we're trying to learn every task, so certainly that's going to be, let's say, as high as 50%, not as high as over 90% like today. Then the rest mostly on reinforcement learning, or, if we get access to good rewards, that would be the next piece of compute, much bigger than it is today. Inference time—I mean, System 2 is slow, but it's not terribly slow. Unless you ask the model to solve protein folding, then probably you can go for a vacation for a month and the model will come back with a solution. A few seconds of compute is okay for inference. items.question: How do you think reward functions for language models can keep improving beyond human annotation?
items.object: Scaling reward functions for language models
items.answer:
We can scale that process as much as we have so far. Many players are realizing the power of human annotation. In fact, deep learning comes thanks to amazing efforts to label a dataset of a million examples. So that way of scaling is one.

But I strongly believe that there might be a bootstrapping effect of the models becoming better at judging their own outputs. Maybe that really is the main hypothesis of reinforcement learning as I see it. I'm not a huge expert in RL, but if checking that something is correct is easier than creating the solution, then we're in business, because the language models will be able to evaluate their own samples more accurately than generate them. Then we have a reinforcement learning loop because we can reinforce the ones that seem more promising and then the model gets better.

Using the model itself as a reward, which incidentally uses language, which is already fuzzy, is one area that I'm excited about. There's a leaderboard of reward models. Some of them use the name, I think, generative reward model. I think that area goes beyond this kind of need for specific task annotations. We might need specific task annotations; then the question is how many labels we'll need.

items.question: How do you understand the apparent violation of the Nyquist theorem by super-resolution generative models?
items.object: Super-resolution generative models and the Nyquist theorem
items.answer:
My undergrad degree—I studied the Nyquist theorem quite heavily, which is funny because we broke it so much. What it says roughly is, if you want to output a certain resolution or frequency in the Fourier domain, you need to sample at half the frequency you want to reconstruct. Otherwise the information is simply not there. If you take an image and sample too little, you will not recover the original frequency.

But look at super-resolution generative models: you input a 32-by-32-pixel image, and it fills in the details in a way that completely violates that principle. I talked to my signal processing teachers about this, and of course it is violating and it is inventing; it's hallucinating. But it's cheating, because it turns out that the world has certain structure that you can learn, which is essentially what all these generative models of images do.

items.question: How do you see AI models developing the ability to self-correct and adapt?
items.object: Emergent self-correction and adaptation in AI models
items.answer:
I agree there's this argument that there are emergence properties. At some point the model might have the capability to self-correct. As soon as it hits that capability, you can see how bootstrapping is trivial. Of course it's not going to be blanket across all, but certainly we're going to see some of this. It's not going to be that dramatic; it's going to be more like, "Hey, this one now emerged," and so on. Once that capability is there, you need to have the algorithms to exploit it, especially these reward models that will be mostly driven by the model itself. Then how many labels, and how are you going to correct the mistakes it might still make? Those are very interesting questions.

Even from a product standpoint they're quite cool. We all play with these models. If they fail, you could just say, "Look, I didn't like this," and the models should adapt. That's where long context also plays into the equation: you have long interactions, you finesse what the model is doing for you. How to enable those capabilities is one of the many exciting future directions in the field.

items.question: How do you decide when specializing an AI model is worthwhile as general-purpose models improve?
items.object: Specialization and general-purpose AI models
items.answer: You want that 20% to keep going up relatively uniformly across the board, so you don't want to over-specialize the models or the research. But the world has very important challenges that are worth solving with specialization. What I tell people in the team and around me is, look, if the problem is worth it, then let's obviously specialize. Probably we can, and we might see more and more bootstrapping from Gemini and these models to a specific solution that the model is going to be thrown away except for maybe cracking protein folding, figuring out nuclear fusion, or modeling the weather—some of the projects currently active in the DeepMind portfolio. You better choose the ones that will matter, because the timeline is such that we'll get there sooner if we specialize in those domains. Perhaps eventually the general model will overtake, but that's probably further away. If it's worth it, do it. We're still going to see this hybrid mode, although more and more taking Gemini and doing something amazing in a narrower domain. That directionality of taking a generalist model and doing something by fine-tuning it is going to loop back as well. Then you're going to do something amazing, let's say in math—we recently did that—and the data or reward model or something that model does will help the main model get better too. It's quite synergistic. If it's important for the world, I'm okay with specialization, for sure.

items.question: How do you assess the criticism that AI research in constrained domains such as mathematics is a dead end for advancing general reasoning?
items.object: Mathematics as a domain for advancing general AI reasoning
items.answer:
There's a validity to that, again going back to the reward-function question. You want to create the most general model or agent or intelligence. It turns out that reward is never perfectly defined by the environment. Even if you go, "Oh no, surviving," it is extremely complicated to compute a reward. You could argue that when you get these rewards from somewhat artificial, interesting but artificial domains, they might not generalize to the real problem, and in that sense it could be a dead end.

Then how you do the research is important. Let's use math as an example. We have access to the reward, but even there it's not that simple. If I'm doing a simple calculation, okay, 4 plus 4 equals 8, I can check that. But now you start thinking, prove this theorem. The proof is either correct or not, but that starts to be more complex to get a precise reward signal, unless you can formalize it. Then there might be bugs in the formalization process or in the engine that checks the math underneath. And even then, if I say 4 plus 4 and instead of saying eight I say 4 plus 4 equals 8, is that correct or not? How do you check correctness? You start to intertwine language explanations.

By trying to solve these problems not in a strictly "the reward is sharp and crisp, did you win or not" way, but also saying, "The reward model just needs to understand what's correct or roughly correct and look at what you wrote and assess," you might start generalizing and moving away from the niche world where reward is perfectly defined, to what's true and what's not true. That's quite complicated. Depending on how you attack the problem, it's definitely not a dead end. Because it's so hard to have a perfect reward when you intertwine language, I think by accident the field will move forward as we discover these more general reward functions, train them better, and they will themselves push the models. Hopefully some sort of self-improvement loop will appear more than it has so far.

items.question: How do you think about AGI as a goal for AI research?
items.object: AGI as a goal for AI research
items.answer:
The contrarian view would be I'm not sure it matters that we achieve AGI. I think it might not look like, "Hey, it's going to be exactly like the cognitive tasks we can do and then we reach parity." It's going to be a distribution of things these models can do or can't do, and that still feels worth pursuing. You see plenty of examples: the model will crack this impossible puzzle in math, and then it will contradict itself trivially somehow.

We need to be ready not to be too fixated on AGI. Still fix the most obviously egregious errors; that's very important because I think they are something profound that is wrong in the models. But I think it's not the exact goal. It's more distributional rather than one point where before we didn't have it and now we do. It's also going to be impossible to get agreement. It's going to be quite a cloud of moments that people might feel it has happened. But it doesn't matter, because the models might be used for amazing things and products and research itself. Bootstrapping research and science is one of the things we're excited about. Google DeepMind's mission has science very much present in the mission statement. That's what motivates me, at least. I don't really care maybe to build AGI in the strict definition, but I understand it. It's a good goal, and I appreciate having a single number to aim for, but it's going to be hard to agree with everyone, as usual.

items.question: How do you think about using AI to expand your own capacity?
items.object: Using AI to scale personal capacity
items.answer:
You adapt as well, sort of like scaling up. Scaling up is very important as you progress in your career: you go from individual contributor writing code to helping others figure out their path.

There's a huge opportunity to scale up thanks to this technology. I've been trying to use it to figure out what has happened in the endless chat rooms I'm in. I'm in London, so when I wake up, California has given me a lot of tokens and long context to process. Personally, you try to figure out how to best use the technology to scale yourself. I talk to quite a few people who are not that much into technology, and all I say is, look, try to figure out how you could collaborate or use it as a tool, because I think that change is definitely coming, no matter what. I might oversimplify it.

items.question: How would you advise children choosing what to study for a future shaped by AI?
items.object: Choosing what to study as AI changes professions
items.answer:
Honestly, from a studying perspective, I feel like there's always your passion element—many of us in the early days did deep learning not because it was the thing to do; it was just what many of us liked to do. I feel I cannot give advice that says find the top professions and choose based on that.

I'll modulate my answer by saying definitely find which aspect is your true passion, or someone you admire, role models, et cetera. What I will say, and I've been saying this for quite a few years, is project how that thing changes with AI. Exploit that. Not everyone will understand the basics of technology, but to be honest, as I was saying, language is the driver, so it's not that hard to understand how this works. I was talking to my sister, who is a teacher, and she used it to create a summary of kids' homework by uploading all the homework. That way of thinking needs to go into quite a few professions.

So, first order, find your passion and follow that. Then second, really embrace some of the tools that are present today.

items.question: Where do you see fruitful research opportunities for someone interested in technology or computer science?
items.object: Research opportunities in AI and its applications
items.answer: If you're into technology or computer science, another fruitful direction is to find the corners of the space that AI hasn't gotten into. Maybe you'll train specialized models, because again it might be worth doing. There are still quite plenty of opportunities. I was just chatting to someone about climate modeling: weather modeling is kind of cracked with deep learning, but climate is quite different. We only have one sample, which is one planet, so it's pretty tricky. Think about what areas could be enhanced. Otherwise, if you like the technology, I think there's quite a lot of LLM research and related work to be done for five or ten years at least. That's probably still a worthwhile way to investigate. If you go into research, there's definitely lots to do.
